faq.a: Abnormal flow creates shear stress on the ascending aorta, and associated connective‑tissue abnormalities weaken the wall, leading to dilation.
faq.q: Why does BAV cause aortic dilation?

faq.a: It can run in families; first‑degree relatives have a 10 % risk, so screening echocardiography is advised.
Mild disease is managed medically; severe stenosis or regurgitation usually requires valve replacement, but balloon valvuloplasty may be a bridge in emergencies.
faq.q: Can BAV be fixed without surgery?

exam: A 28‑year‑old male presents with a harsh systolic murmur and mild dyspnoea – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform focused transthoracic echo to confirm valve morphology and assess gradient; it guides urgency of referral.

How does BAV predispose to infective endocarditis and what prophylaxis is recommended in low‑resource settings? — Turbulent flow damages endothelium, allowing bacterial adherence; give oral penicillin prophylaxis for high‑risk dental procedures if rheumatic disease co‑exists.

A patient with known BAV has an aortic diameter of 48 mm on echo – what management plan should you outline? — Refer for surgical evaluation for aortic root repair; monitor every 6‑12 months if surgery not immediately available.

Explain why a patient with BAV and hypertension may develop severe stenosis earlier than a normotensive counterpart. — Hypertension adds pressure load, accelerating calcific degeneration and leaflet stiffening.

During a febrile illness, a patient’s murmur changes from systolic to a new diastolic component – what does this suggest and what immediate action is needed? — Development of regurgitation suggests acute endocarditis; obtain blood cultures and start empiric antibiotics.

What are the key differences on physical exam between BAV‑related aortic stenosis and rheumatic aortic stenosis? — BAV often has a midsystolic ejection click and a crescendo‑decrescendo murmur; rheumatic disease may show associated mitral stenosis and a more “soft” murmur.

In a setting without echocardiography, how would you monitor a patient with known BAV for progression? — Use serial clinical assessment (symptoms, blood pressure, pulse pressure), chest X‑ray for aortic size, and ECG for LV hypertrophy.
Why is anticoagulation generally avoided in isolated BAV unless there is another indication? — Valve leaflets are not prosthetic; anticoagulation adds bleeding risk without preventing progression.
ai.title: Bicuspid Aortic Valve
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is a congenital malformation where the aortic valve has two leaflets instead of three. It predisposes to early valve dysfunction, aortic dilation and infective endocarditis, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: The aortic valve normally has three cusps. In BAV two cusps are fused, most often the right‑left coronary cusps. This structural change alters flow, creating turbulence and stress on the valve and ascending aorta.

b: Stenosis develops from calcific degeneration; usually before age 60 in BAV vs >70 in tricuspid valves
Regurgitation results from cusp prolapse or aortic root dilation
Aortic diameter >45 mm in BAV signals high risk of dissection
sections.p: BAV can be isolated or part of a spectrum of connective‑tissue disorders. The main clinical problems are aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, aortic root dilation and infective endocarditis.

b: Early systolic ejection murmur radiating to the neck suggests stenosis
Diastolic decrescendo murmur at left sternal border suggests regurgitation
Pulse pressure widening >60 mmHg may hint at severe regurgitation
sections.p: Patients may present with exertional dyspnoea, chest pain, syncope or a murmur. In low‑resource hospitals, rheumatic heart disease and hypertension accelerate valve damage, while limited imaging may delay diagnosis.

t.b: Confirms valve morphology and quantifies stenosis/regurgitation; if unavailable, use focused cardiac ultrasound on a portable device
Shows aortic root enlargement or pulmonary congestion; useful when echo not possible
Detects left ventricular hypertrophy or strain patterns; helps gauge severity

b: Ask about syncope, exertional chest pain and family sudden cardiac death
Check blood pressure in both arms – a >10 mmHg difference may indicate aortic arch involvement
Look for peripheral signs of endocarditis (Osler nodes, splinter hemorrhages) in febrile patients
sections.p: When you hear a murmur in a young adult, always consider BAV, especially if there is a family history of early valve disease or aortic aneurysm.

b: Assuming a systolic murmur is always benign in young adults
Neglecting to measure aortic dimensions when stenosis is mild
Prescribing anticoagulation without confirming infective endocarditis
sections.p: Mistaking BAV‑related murmur for isolated hypertension or rheumatic disease leads to missed surveillance of the aorta.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe chest pain radiating to the back (possible aortic dissection)
Fever with a new murmur (suspect endocarditis)
